title: Daily Practice App for Pharmacutical Calculations
text:
It is a common issue that students entering pharmacy programs struggle mightily with the calculations required by the program. Certainly, any math educator will flag weak fundamentals as the most common reason students struggle in mathematics, and pharmacy students are no different. While the math required by pharmacy programs is relatively low-level, it’s embedded in a more difficult scientific context, might not have been seen by the student in years, and just a small part of a program that keeps a punishing pace.
The “proper” answer for weak math fundamentals is for the student to diligently go back and practice each fundamental skill, starting with basic arithmetic and slowly working their way up to the skills relevant for their current goals. This is not practical advice for a student struggling with math in a pharmacy program, however. Instead, we focus more on just-in-time intervention, attempting to shore up a student’s basic skills as they become relevant to the more demanding calculation problems at hand, before sending them off to face the exam and then pivoting to the next topic. This approach, although necessary, leads to some painful consequences for the student later on.
Under this just-in-time approach, a student is constantly in crisis in math, as each new topic demands a new set of skills and solution process. Old material must be left by the wayside as they turn their focus to the new crises at hand, naturally falling into a “cram and move on” routine with math that never lets them develop long-term retention or fluency with the material. This is an approach that will surely be familiar to educators at the high-school and undergraduate level. For students who will later go on to be accepted to pharmacy school, though, they can survive this routine at the undergraduate and high-school levels, where courses are slower paced, final exams might not be cumulative, and the content can be safely forgotten once the course is finished.
In pharmacy school, however, none of these things hold true. The NAPLEX, the licensure exam for prospective pharmacists in the US, waits for these students after they complete their programs, and it demands long-term retention of all the content covered during their program. To prepare students, pharmacy programs will commonly have cumulative review checkpoints throughout their curriculum to ensure that a student has retained (or recrammed) a basic level of understanding of pharmaceutical calculations. For example, a calculation refresher class during P3 and a board review program in P4. Unfortunately, this often just recreates the cramming cycle, and doesn’t necessarily lead to long-term retention of the material.
For other parts of the pharmacy school curriculum, such as the Top 300 Drugs, students can rely on spaced-repetition programs such as Anki to develop long-term retention of the relevant material, but Anki is a flashcard-based program, and so it is not readily applicable to calculation-based material. Instead, calculation problems are typically given out as homework as those types of problems are covered in their respective courses, or large review packets are handed out as preparation for cumulative exams or NAPLEX prep courses. In both cases, the calculation problems are not delivered in a method consistent with spaced-repetition approaches to long-term retention of skills, nor is it reasonable to expect an instructor in such a course to deliver individualized spaced-repetition plans for each student. This practice app is meant to fill that gap.

title: Daily Practice App for Pharmacutical Calculations
text:
Design rationale
The core of this program is a practice problem bank combined with an Anki-inspired scheduler. Using Claude Opus 5.5, practice problem templates were generated for each topic subdivided by solution process (called skills in the program). Practice problems were generated using random input numbers according to realistic ranges for their problem, and then solutions were generated using custom python programs to ensure accuracy.
When a student first opens the program, they’re asked to select from a list of topics to build their deck. More topics can be added to their deck later, which allows students studying for review or board prep to select all topics, and students using the program alongside a course can slowly add new topics as they go. The student also selects a desired number of problems per day, with a recommended amount typically being three or four problems. This is an intentional change to the Anki design, where missing a day can lead to the load for the next day being unreasonably large. Here, the load is kept to a fixed amount with an optional catch-up mode that can give the student up to 50% additional problems if they have outstanding skills due.
This program uses a simplified version of the Anki FSRS algorithm to schedule problems based on the expected likelihood of a student getting that particular skill correct. The algorithm uses a statistic called “stability” to schedule each skill. Stability is roughly defined as the number of days after seeing the skill that it takes for a student to fall to a 90% expected probability of successfully solving the skill. Once a skill falls to its 90% solve probability, it becomes due, and the algorithm will start trying to show that skill again.
The program updates stability based on both whether a student got the latest instance of that skill correct or not, as well as an Anki-inspired difficulty rating for that problem. If a student gets a question wrong, they’re asked if they missed the problem due to an obvious mistake (slip) or if they were stuck on the problem altogether. If a student gets a problem correct, they’re asked to rate the problem as either hard, good, or easy. This rating gives a multiplier to stability, causing stability to shrink or grow by different amounts.
In addition, worked solutions for each problem are provided. These solutions were also generated by Claude Opus 5.5 from solution templates developed by the author. Solutions can be viewed both before an answer is given and after with an early peek counted as a stuck question.
Altogether, this app is designed to keep the student’s cognitive load to an absolute minimum while still providing them with an interleaved, spaced repetition practice regimen. The student never has to search for practice problems, try to keep track of which skills need attention, or worry about looking up solutions. The student is given a personalized study regimen that fits their schedule and adapts as they grow, while only requiring a ~15 minute time investment every day they choose to study.

title: Daily Practice App for Pharmacutical Calculations
text:
How AI was used
This project fell under a level 1 AI-assisted educational project where the focus is on keeping AI involvement separate from the student experience. AI was used heavily in the question bank development and app coding. To ensure high-quality questions that fully encapsulated the pharmaceutical calculations needed by students in a pharmacy programs, and I began by writing up a list of the relevant topics. Then, for each topic, they were divided into skills based on the solution processes needed. For example, dilution and evaporation problems, while seemingly divided into two separate skills, actually follow nearly identical solution processes: solve a single variable equation for c_1 v_1 = c_2 v_2. Single-solution problems, on the other hand, were divided into three skills depending on if the student needed to identify concentration, amount of drug or total, or amount of solvent. Once the list of topics and skills was finalized, Claude Opus 5.5 was utilized to create roughly a dozen different problem templates per skill (changing the relevant drug or scenario). Then, for each template, five or six individual problems were generated to make up the problem bank.
To avoid AI-hallucinations, the individual problems used randomly generated input numbers generated by the AI to fall within reasonable expected ranges for the template’s drugs. The solutions to each problem, on the other hand, were generated programmatically from the input numbers using an AI-created Python program for each problem template. I then checked an examplar from each skill to check for any obvious errors. To further ensure the accuracy of problems, I engage in a daily routine of solving my own practice questions to identify bad questions or otherwise check the quality of the app.
Claude was also used to generate the worked solutions for each problem template. For each skill, an examplar solution was developed by Claude, based off of example solution processes I developed. These exemplars were then presented to me and checked for accuracy and style, and the style point in particular is where Claude seems to struggle the most. I would often make changes to have the solution processes flow better or focus only on the key points of the problem. Once a solution template was approved, Claude would fill in the template for each associated problem.
In addition to the question bank, Claude Opus 5.5 was heavily used to develop the code for the website. As before, I engage in regular testing of the app to ensure all features work correctly.
The app was also able to be further tested using Claude by way of simulation. Claude was able to run simulations to identify bugs and test our algorithm against other algorithms. For example, an initial implementation of the algorithm had stability grow without limit, and would quickly lead to strong skills never being checked up on.



A bug in an early version of a the algorithm where stability was uncapped.


It was also possible to run simulations of student usage of the app under different assumptions to fine-tune the algorithm or test against other algorithms, such as a full implementation of the FSRS algorithm.



A chart showing a simulation of a student’s daily problems by topic if that student added all topics to their deck immediately upon starting the program.





A heatmap of topics covered by week under different breakdowns of topics by skills.


It was even possible to generate entire cohorts of students with different study and app-usage habits to test their performance under a variety of study methods, with a focus on app usage vs. cramming. The results for one cohort of simulated students is shown below.

Crammer: studies every day in the week before an exam, otherwise about a third of days. Fading: starts nearly daily and drops off over the term. Do note that these simulations used a very simplified mathematical model for skill decay, and these results shouldn’t be compared to actual student performance on an exam. The simulated results mostly confirm the common knowledge that more time spent studying results in higher scores, but app usage divides up 22 expected study hours into 15-minute/day sized chunks, and it improves retention 30 days later over cramming-relient strategies. Both of these aspects are highly desirable for our target student population (extremely busy pharmacy students who need to retain information for boards), and so this simulation is taken as a positive signal. The dismal course homework only scores assume a student who does the assigned homework and then never reviews that information again, so this is also expected as baseline performance.

title: A Gradual Release of Responsibility
text:
In education, there’s a concept, first introduced by David Pearson and Margaret Gallagher, called the gradual release of responsibility. This is a pedagogical method wherein the instructor initially holds all the responsibility for learning, and students are gradually given more and more responsibility until they are learning independently. In a math setting, let’s say, learning how to complete the square to solve quadratic equations, this might look like

The instructor works through an entire problem showing each step of the completing the square algorithm.
The instructor works through another completing the square problem, but this time, they stop before a couple of steps and ask the students what the next step should be.
The instructor works through another problem, and asks the students what comes next for each step.
The instructor gives one more problem, and has the students solve the problem while they observe.
The instructor gives homework to be completed independently.

And so, the responsibility for learning initially rested entirely on the instructor’s shoulders, but more and more responsibility was handed off to the student until they were expected to complete the homework by themselves. This is sometimes referred to as “I do, we do, you do” instruction.
I believe this idea has applications to deciding how to implement AI into the classroom. Here, there are three entities that can hold some amount of responsibility for student learning: the instructor, the AI, and the student. Getting the balance right is critical, as many educators have learned.



Takehome midterms grades vs. in-person final grades for Brown University professor Roberto Serrano’s ECON 1170 course.


The key is that responsibility must be gradually released from the instructor to the AI and to the student, based on student expertise and motivation. In lower level courses, where students are often forced to take these courses with little to no choice, AI interaction should be extremely restrained. Up through undergraduate introductory or general education courses, AI should mostly be a tool for the instructor to implement tools they might not be able to do otherwise. Once a student has been able to start a degree path and invest time developing their expertise in the subject, then they should be able to shoulder the burden of more unrestricted AI usage, although it should be with well-defined objectives and limitations. Unrestricted AI usage, insofar as it has anything to do with accredited education, should be restricted to students working with a great deal of expertise and motivation. A graduate student researcher, for instance, might well utilize AI in an unrestricted manner to learn new tools, statistical methods, and gain a deeper overview of their field, and this is good AI usage! But it only comes into play when a student is able to take responsibility for their own learning, like we expect for graduate students. Earlier than that, then I fear the results of Professor Serrano’s infamous ECON 1170 course are the rule rather than the exception.
I propose the following framework to help differentiate different levels of AI responsibility.

Level 1: No direct AI/student interaction. All responsibility remains with the instructor.
Level 2: AI is used to interpret student responses. Almost all responsibility remains with the instructor.
Level 3: AI is able to reply to student responses within the scope of a well-defined exchange. The instructor defines system prompts for the AI and objective briefings for the student,
Level 4: AI may be used freely to investigate. The instructor may set an assignment scope, but all remaining responsibility for learning rests with the student.

At level 1, the AI is a nonentity in the learning exchange. If AI is used, it is used solely to develop a tool, and the instructor bears all responsibility for the accuracy and content of this tool. This is where, I believe, the bulk of potential for AI usage lies. Letting instructors develop tools that weren’t feasible for them before. My pharmacy calculation practice app is one such example. It was always theoretically possible for me to make this tool, but I never would have found the time to develop it on my own. While AI was used heavily to develop the question bank, I still bear the responsibility to the accuracy of these questions, which I tried to ensure by programmatically generating solutions from problem inputs, checking initial questions by hand, editing solution templates, and continuing to use the tool itself daily so that I can catch other potential problems I missed. The student never actually interacts with the AI.
At level 2, AI can be used to interpret student work, but the AI does not reply to the student. We might consider using AI to identify and sort mistakes in student calculations as an example of a level 2 AI usage. We’ve started to release some responsibility to the AI, but the student experienced hasn’t changed from level 1. They’re still doing the same work, and the difference here is how we’re interacting with that work. While I don’t think AI should ever take sole responsibility for grading student work, modern LLMs offer an ability to investigate, interpret, and categorize student work that hasn’t existed. For example, it would be possible to save and scan a semester’s worth of student math work and then analyze the work and sort the errors into conceptual, procedural, and computational errors. This data can then be used to identify pain points in pedagogy or areas of weakness in student prerequisite skills.
Level 3 is where the student and the AI are finally allowed to interact directly. This is the level that every new edtech company under the sun is trying to develop tools for, and this is the level where we must take the most care as educators.



A staged screenshot showing a customer asking a McDonald’s chatbot to write a python program


Here, it’s very easy for a student to overstep the bounds of the assignment, either to disengage with the work altogether or to undercut the desired learning experience of the assignment. Unless you have students you think are motivated enough by the material to remain within the guidelines you set for the assignment, you might restrict these assignments to in-class only or require logs of student interactions. Level 3 assignments have a very wide range in how much responsibility rests with the AI. At the lowest level, the interaction might consist of a single prompt and response between the student and AI. At the higher ranges, the interaction might look more like a tutoring session. The R-statistics-analysis-session is a good example of a higher range level 3 interaction. At this level, it is critical to define exactly what your expectations are for both the student and the AI. For the AI, we might craft a strong system prompt that defines the setting of the interaction, the steps and expected student responses at each step, as well as instructions to redirect the student back to the assignment if they start to go outside the boundaries. For the student, we want a similarly strong orientation brief that lays out the exact expectations of the student at each step of the interaction and what the end-product of the interaction should be.
Finally, level 4 is where the student bears total responsibility for their own learning, with the instructor only providing the assignment parameters, and might be best thought of as self-study. My personal attempts to learn R, which lead to the aforementioned R analysis session framework, might fall under this category. I started that project because I wanted to learn R for my own benefit, and so I was sufficiently trusted not to seek shortcuts. I also had the relevant expertise, having a master’s degree in mathematics, to be able to guide the AI when it started to get hung up on irrelevant points. Without the motivation, you can’t trust a student not to seek shortcuts, and without the expertise, you can’t trust the student to know when the AI is hallucinating or getting hung up on the wrong thing. Thus, it’s difficult to justify allowing this sort of interaction in an actual course below the graduate level, where students are already largely responsible for their own learning. Insofar as a level 4 assignment might appear in a primary, secondary, or undergraduate curriculum, I can only imagine it working as some sort of low-stakes, participation-only assignment, but should otherwise be avoided.
With the framework set up, while there’s a lot of pressure for edtech companies, administrations, and AI hype guys to jump right into level 3 or level 4 work, I believe these assignments should be given very sparingly, with well-defined boundaries for both the AI and the student. If we apply the “I do, we do, you do” framework to education as a whole, it’s obvious that most work through high school level is “I do” work. The instructor is still responsible for their education. The students are taking classes required by their school with very little independent choice. They learn to do trigonometry or write an essay by following strict formulas. They read books that are assigned by their teachers. None of this, in a vacuum, is bad. The “I do” stage is very important, both within a single lesson and within education itself. A student has to learn how to learn before they can go out and do it effectively on their own, and we see this progression in undergraduate education. A student slowly picks their major, works through upper level courses, and finally completes a bachelor’s thesis; they work through the “we do” stage, gradually taking more and more responsibility for their own learning. And then when a student progresses to grad school, they’re often in a situation where they’re solely responsible for learning the material.
Viewing education as a whole through this lense, I believe it becomes much clearly when each level is applicable. Levels 1 and 2 are ultimately about enabling the instructor to do more. The instructor still bears the responsibility of learning, and so the bulk of AI usage at the “I do” stage of education should keep the responsibility for learning on the instructor’s shoulders. Level 3 work might occasionally be used for higher-level work, but you must release that responsibility with the educational well-being of the students in mind. As the student moves into higher education, they start to inherit more responsibility for their education. As such, I believe they can be trusted with higher level assignments. An upper level biology major, for instance, might get quite a lot out of the R statistics learning framework in a research course.
And by the time we release nearly all responsibility for learning to the student, students working on independent research or students in graduate courses, they should be well-prepared and motivated to get a lot out of free exploration with AI.
